# Regular Expressions (regex) {.maize}

## Where we left off

Suppose we wish to anonymize phone numbers in survey results

```{r}
a1 <- "Home: 507-645-5489"
a2 <- "Cell: 219.917.9871"
a3 <- "My work phone is 507-202-2332"
a4 <- "I don't have a phone"
info <- c(a1, a2, a3, a4)
```

::: {.nonincremental}
Last time: literal matches, `.`, and `[]`. Today: special patterns, anchors, alternatives, and repetition.
:::

## Visualizing matches

The helper function `str_view()` finds regex matches

```{r}
str_view(a1, "5")
```

## `.` match any character

Find a "-" and any (.) character that follows

```{r eval=require('stringr')}
str_view(a1, "-.")
```

## `[]` match any occurence

Find any numbers between 0 and 9

```{r }
str_view(a1, "[0123456789]")
```

## `[]` match any occurence

Find any numbers between 2 and 7

```{r }
str_view(a1, "[2-7]")
```


## Special patterns 

There are a number of special patterns that match more than one character

::: nonincremental 
- `\\d` - digit
- `\\s` - white space
- `\\w` - word
- `\\t` - tab
- `\\n` - newline
:::

. . . 

```{r }
str_view(a1, "\\d")
```

::: aside
Outside of R, these would be single back slashes.
:::

## Caution!

```{r }
str_view(a1, "\\w")
```

## `[^]` match any occurence except

ANYTHING BUT numbers between 2 and 7

```{r }
str_view(a1, "[^2-7]")
```

::: aside
Common pitfall: forgetting the brackets
:::

## Anchors

Anchors look for matches at the start `^` or end `$`

```{r}
#| echo: false
str_view(info)
```

::: panel-tabset

### Entries that start with a digit

```{r}
str_view(info, "^\\d")
```


### Entries that end with a digit

```{r}
str_view(info, "\\d$")
```

:::

## Use regex in `str_detect`, `str_sub`, etc: 

```{r }
str_view(info)
```

```{r }
str_detect(info, "\\d")
```

```{r }
str_replace_all(info, "\\d", "X")
```

## Alternative patterns

`|` allows you to match one or more alternative patterns

```{r}
str_view(info, "^H|C")
```


## "Fixing" the order of operations

Why are these different?

::::: columns
::: {.column .nonincremental width="50%"}
```{r}
str_view(info, "^H|C.")
```
:::


::: {.column .nonincremental width="50%"}
```{r}
str_view(info, "^(H|C).")
```
:::
:::::

## Repetition

You can search for a pattern followed by the number  of matches

::::: columns
::: {.column .nonincremental width="50%"}
- `?`: 0 or 1
- `+`: 1 or more
- `*`: 0 or more
- `{n}`: exactly n times
- `{n,}`: n or more times
- `{,m}`: at most m times
- `{n,m}`: between n and m times
:::

::: {.column .nonincremental .fragment width="50%"}
Example: detect three digits in a row

```{r}
str_view(a1, "\\d{3}")
```

:::
:::::

# Intro to Text Analysis {.maize}

## Text Analysis

Up to this point, we've been thinking of string data as a column in our dataset: 

  - Names
  - Phone numbers
  - Addresses
  - Course titles
  - etc. 

. . . 

which are all relatively short and structured. We can extract meaning from them using relatively simple functions and "know what we're looking for".

## {background-image="../img/coursera-data-sci.png"}


## Sometimes, text data is more unstructured

Random (?) sample of 26,882 reviews of coursera courses

```{r}
en_coursera_reviews <- read_csv("../../data/en_coursera_sample.csv") # https://stat220-f26.github.io/data/en_coursera_sample.csv
en_coursera_reviews
```

::: aside
Source: [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/septa97/100k-courseras-course-reviews-dataset/data)
:::

*Note:* may need to install `tidytext` and `stopwords` packages

## Sometimes, text data is more unstructured

```{r}
en_coursera_reviews %>%
  filter(str_detect(Review, "ggplot")) %>%
  pull(Review)
``` 

## {.center}

::::: columns
::: {.column .nonincremental width="50%"}

![](https://juliasilge.github.io/tidytext/reference/figures/tidytext.png){width="60%"}
:::

:::{.column .nonincremental width="50%"}
- Functions for text analysis that follow tidy data principles

- *Not* part of the `tidyverse`, but plays well with other packages

```{r}
library(tidytext)
```

:::
:::::

## Some notation

*document*: an observation of text data (in this case, an abstract)

. . . 

*corpus*: collection of many documents

. . . 

*token*: a unit of analysis within the document (typically a word, but could be a sentence or a line or a pair of words, etc.)

## Text as tidy data

1. *tokenize* each document
    - Each *row* in the dataset is a token
2. Remove *stopwords*
    - Words like "the" and "is" typically aren't interesting
    - Makes the dataset smaller and easier to work with
3. Count the tokens
4. (optional) *fancy count* the tokens
    - Standardize based on total number of tokens
    - How common is a token *relative to other documents*
    - How common are "good words" or "bad words"

## `unnest_tokens()`

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
- `tbl`: our data
- `output`: what should the output column be called?
- `input`: what column do we tokenize?
- `token`: default is "word" but can also be "ngrams", "sentences", "lines", "paragraphs", etc.
- `to_lower`: should tokens be converted to lowercase
:::
::: {.column .nonincremental width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
unnest_tokens(
  tbl,
  output,
  input,
  token = "words",
  to_lower = TRUE,
  drop = TRUE,
  ...
)
```
:::
:::::


## Tokenize

```{r}
library(tidytext)
en_coursera_reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(output = word, input = Review) |>
  select(CourseId, word)
```


## Stopwords

```{r}
get_stopwords(source = "stopwords-iso") |> pull(word)
```

## `anti_join`

![](../slides/img/anti-join.gif)

## Remove stopwords

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "3"

en_coursera_reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(output = word, input = Review) |>
  anti_join(get_stopwords(source = "stopwords-iso"), by = "word") |>
  select(CourseId, word)
```

## Filter to include only data science courses

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"

en_coursera_reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(output = word, input = Review) |>
  anti_join(get_stopwords(source = "stopwords-iso"), by = "word") |>
  filter(str_detect(CourseId, "data-science")) |> 
  select(CourseId, word)
```

## Count the tokens

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| code-line-numbers: "5-6|7|8-10"

en_coursera_reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(output = word, input = Review) |>
  anti_join(get_stopwords(source = "stopwords-iso"), by = "word") |>
  filter(str_detect(CourseId, "data-science")) |> 
  group_by(CourseId) %>%
  count(word) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 10) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(word, n))) + 
  geom_col() + 
  facet_wrap(~CourseId, scales = "free_y", nrow = 2) + 
  labs(
    y = "Word"
  ) + 
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 8))
```

# Bigrams {.maize}

## Tokens don't have to be single words

A *bigram* is a pair of words that appear next to each other. Use `token = "ngrams"` and `n = 2`.

```{r}
en_coursera_reviews |>
  filter(review_id == 6) |>
  pull(Review)
```

```{r}
en_coursera_reviews |>
  filter(review_id == 6) |>
  unnest_tokens(output = bigram, input = Review, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  select(review_id, bigram)
```

. . .

Each word (except the first and last) appears in *two* bigrams.

## Most common bigrams

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
en_coursera_reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(output = bigram, input = Review, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  filter(!is.na(bigram)) |>
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(bigram, n))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(y = "Bigram", x = "Number of reviews")
```

. . .

We did *not* remove stopwords here. `anti_join()` on bigrams would not work anyway, because no bigram is a stopword.

## If we do want to remove stopwords

Remove stopwords from each review *first*, then make bigrams from the cleaned reviews.

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "1-5|7-10"
coursera_reviews <- en_coursera_reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(word, Review) |>
  anti_join(get_stopwords(source = "stopwords-iso"), by = "word") |>
  group_by(CourseId, review_id) |>
  summarize(review_clean = paste(word, collapse = " "), .groups = "drop")

coursera_reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(output = bigram, input = review_clean, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  filter(!is.na(bigram)) |>
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE)
```

## Which should we use?

::: {.nonincremental}
- Removing stopwords: **what are people talking about?** (`machine learning`, `data science`, `programming assignments`)
- Keeping stopwords: **what does the language look like?** (`this course`, `a lot`, `thank you`)
:::

. . .

It depends on the question. For the next piece, we will keep them.

## Which word comes next?

Split each bigram into its first and second word:

```{r}
bigrams <- en_coursera_reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(output = bigram, input = Review, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  filter(!is.na(bigram)) |>
  separate(bigram, into = c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ")

bigrams |>
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE)
```

. . .

What word most often comes after `data`?

```{r}
bigrams |>
  filter(word1 == "data") |>
  count(word2, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 5)
```

# For reference {.maize}

Not covered in class, but here if you want to use them in your own analysis.

## Removing stopwords: a different dictionary

`stopwords::stopwords_getsources()` lists the available dictionaries, and they give different results.

```{r}
coursera_reviews2 <- en_coursera_reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(word, Review) |>
  anti_join(get_stopwords(source = "snowball"), by = "word") |>
  group_by(CourseId, review_id) |>
  summarize(review_clean = paste(word, collapse = " "), .groups = "drop")
```

Original review:

```{r}
en_coursera_reviews |> filter(review_id == 6) |> pull(Review)
```

Clean review (`stopwords-iso`):

```{r}
coursera_reviews |> filter(review_id == 6) |> pull(review_clean)
```

Clean review (`snowball`):

```{r}
coursera_reviews2 |> filter(review_id == 6) |> pull(review_clean)
```

## tf-idf

Idea: how common are certain tokens *relative to the rest of the documents in the corpus*?

. . .

tf(t,d) = "term frequency": what proportion of document d is term t?

. . .

idf = "inverse document frequency": log-scaled inverse fraction of documents that contain the term

$$\text{idf} = \log \frac{\text{number of documents}}{\text{number of documents containing term t}}$$

. . .

$$\text{tf-idf(t, d)} = \text{tf(t, d)} \times \text{idf(t)}$$

## tf-idf in R

Highest tf-idf words are used a lot within a document, and rarely in other documents.

```{r}
en_coursera_reviews |>
  unnest_tokens(word, Review) |>
  count(review_id, word) |>
  bind_tf_idf(word, review_id, n) |>
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))
```
